title: [Bug]: Federated CloudID leaking on public lookup-server callback
body:
# Summary

*added by @participant2 18th March*

For the final state, closing-statement, please see https://github.com/nextcloud/server/issues/51335#issuecomment-2733919135 at the bottom of this issue.

As a summary 7th March 11:36PM CET this issue here has been raised having spotted outside calls by the lookup-server (https://github.com/nextcloud/lookup-server/ centrally run by Nextcloud GmbH) showing federated cloudIDs on the URLs of the inbound http (not https) call after updating the server to the latest maintenance release (February 2025 releases for 29, 30 and 31). 

The root cause analysis showed that 
*  **Triggering point:** A business logic error introduced by the maintenance releases of February 2025 led to calls to the lookup-server for any user created before Feb 2021 or users created afterwards that at any point in time in the past had a profile field actively set to "published" (which means publish to public address-book)
* **Actual issue this ticket is about:** A business logic error on the lookup-server led to first doing a identity proof call (see first paragraph of this issue) via http instead of first checking if there has been any record in the database also not doing this via https instead

This matter has been resolved (again, see https://github.com/nextcloud/server/issues/51335#issuecomment-2733919135 for details) by taking down the lookup-server endpoint to not accept or expose data, ensure the maintenance releases for March were released soon after the root cause got identified blocking the calls to the lookup-server and due to the identification of a deletion-error (not deleting the cloudID) also deleting all data the business logic error failed to delete (empty records just having a cloudID but no other fields fileld)

---

### ⚠️ This issue respects the following points: ⚠️

- [x] This is a **bug**, not a question or a configuration/webserver/proxy issue.
- [x] This issue is **not** already reported on [Github](https://github.com/nextcloud/server/issues?q=is%3Aopen+is%3Aissue+label%3Abug) OR [Nextcloud Community Forum](https://<redacted-host>/) _(I've searched it)_.
- [x] Nextcloud Server **is** up to date. See [Maintenance and Release Schedule](https://github.com/nextcloud/server/wiki/Maintenance-and-Release-Schedule) for supported versions.
- [x] I agree to follow Nextcloud's [Code of Conduct](https://nextcloud.com/contribute/code-of-conduct/).

### Bug description

After the release of Nextcloud 31.0.0, a user reported suspicious activity on their Nextcloud instance after installing the update: https://bsd.network/@niels/114106538216130985

These request contain the usernames of the instance's users and target:
```
65.21.231.50 - - [07/Mar/2025:20:20:00 +0000] "GET /ocs/v2.php/identityproof/key/<USERID> HTTP/1.1" 301 169 "-" "GuzzleHttp/7"
```

All requests originate from 65.21.231.50. This indicates that PII was transmitted to a third party--in this case Nextcloud--without sufficient user consent. Depending on the selected userId, this data included full names and email addresses.

Being pointed to the issue, I was able to identify jobs named `OCA\LookupServerConnector\BackgroundJobs\RetryJob` as the root cause of these requests.

On all affected nextcloud instances I operate this behavior started exactly after the upgrade to 31.0.0. From the codebase it remains unclear what triggered the behavior. However, several functions around lookupServerUpload handling were refactored or altered in the meantime.

Auditing the configuration did not clarify which user settings may relate to exposure, as affected accounts also included dedicated accounts for, e.g., presentation machines at a conference not used by humans.

By instrumenting related source files, it was established that the configuration setting `'files_sharing', 'lookupServerUploadEnabled'` ultimately enabling the datasharing triggering external requests is found under the Path:

```
Admin Settings -> Sharing -> Federated Cloud Sharing -> Allow people to publish their data to a global and public address book
```

Given that the implication of this setting is that the data of several users who had certainly not given explicit consent to the data transfer was shared with a third party (Nextcloud), the labeling of this configuration setting is, at best, dangerously misleading and at worst hiding its actual implications.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Upgrade from Nextcloud v30.0.6 to v31.0.0
2. Wait for the regular cronjob to run
3. Within seconds of the first `OCA\LookupServerConnector\BackgroundJobs\RetryJob` job for a user, a request from `65.21.231.50` will be made to `/ocs/v2.php/identityproof/key/<USERID>`, demonstrating that data was shared with a third party.


### Expected behavior

- The global `"lookupServerUploadEnabled"` setting should remain `NO` after an upgrade, and **NO** user data should be shared with third parties without users' or operators' consent.
- The setting for `"lookupServerUploadEnabled"` should be descriptively labeled, require confirmation, and make the implications of being enabled clear

### Nextcloud Server version

31

### Operating system

Debian/Ubuntu

### PHP engine version

None

### Web server

None

### Database engine version

None

### Is this bug present after an update or on a fresh install?

None

### Are you using the Nextcloud Server Encryption module?

None

### What user-backends are you using?

- [x] Default user-backend _(database)_
- [x] LDAP/ Active Directory
- [ ] SSO - SAML
- [ ] Other

### Configuration report

```json

```

### List of activated Apps

```shell

```

### Nextcloud Signing status

```shell

```

### Nextcloud Logs

```json

```

### Additional info

Please understand that the turn of events is extremely unfortunate. I will have to evaluate over the next 72h whether this event falls under Art. 33 III DSGVO.

I expect Nextcloud GmbH to perform due diligence in this matter as well. This includes:

- Ensuring that all potentially unintentionally leaked data is deleted
- Ensuring that this data is not re-shared to third parties or made publicly available
- Sharing documentation on the above two steps and a post-mortem with the Nextcloud community and the responsible DPA

**Note on HackerOne Submission:** On Mattermost and in Nextcloud's security reporting information on GitHub, a submission of security sensitive events is requested via HackerOne.  I decided to not follow this recommendation for the following reasons:
- I do not consent to the terms and conditions of HackerOne, but believe that this issue is critically important for the community
- The leak/"vulnerability" (or rather: 'unintentional feature') can be mitigated by operators, if they set the aforementioned config setting to off; Delaying publication would, hence, expose users further.
- Technically, in this case, the not necessarily authorized collector of data is Nextcloud GmbH

The more I look at this, it indeed seems to be related to a rather old PR (4-years-ish) only merged recently:

https://github.com/nextcloud/server/issues/25290

- The default settings were probably in place without causing the observed behavior for a long time
- The patch being merged led to user data actually being publicly exchanged

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
You can define sane defaults for related config values before upgrading with:
```
php occ config:app:set --value no files_sharing lookupServerUploadEnabled
php occ config:app:set --value no files_sharing lookupServerEnabled
```

These will not be overridden by the upgrade.

If you have upgraded already, you can use these commands instead of clicking your way through the UI.

comments.author: participant4
comments.body:
The lookup server running on <redacted-host> uses HTTP, not HTTPS, to submit its API requests. This means that login names travel unencrypted over the wire. This seems to be hardcoded behaviour.

"Allow[ing] people to publish their data to a global and public address book" is not what happened here. The way that is phrased means that the admin allows users to choose to publish data, but data was published for a local user that hadn't logged in directly for several months and thus couldn't possibly have consented to any data sharing. Should that option have read "Forcibly upload users' data to a global and public address book"?

## Also as a general info 

in particular for @reporter since you raised the issue, I was able to get a hold of our CEO to align on the exact next step and I will talk to the developers on Monday (tomorrow) to: **implement a general stop sign for all the above mentioned issues to make it into the next release** which is currently being build, hence RC2 for v30 and v31. This means Nextcloud server won't send any of the above mentioned data to the lookup-server anymore, neither the details user data nor the ID.

Currently no data is stored or exposed as mentioned in a comment above since the lookup-server got patches to not accept or expose data on its API endpoint any longer.

So this comes with the upside that while I can't tell you a release date yet (need to talk to developers during the work week first) we will ship a release very soon having this behavior removed effectively. The downside (I am aware this depends on peoples point of view) is that you will need to know a federated cloud ID so the price tag to pay is bad UX for federated sharing. So we will be working on coming up and implementing a good solution for enabling users again to search for federated cloud IDs and yes, you already mentioned it @reporter there is no issue if the solution works consent-based and of course the deletion of the data needs to work reliable as well.

comments.author: participant8
comments.body:
> [@participant4](https://github.com/participant4) to come up with a clear description for the toggle might be a bit of a challenge and can surely be improved. Beware that the fields in the user's profile have a visibility setting each. So users can infact decide on each individually what to publish.

First of all, not cool, guys, not cool! And don't get me wrong. I'm not against the federation feature, and if a central discovery/directory/lookup server makes it easier to use, then I'm all for providing such a service.

BUT!!! There should be a main toggle above all these federation-related toggles that allows users to turn on/off *all* of these features at once. And that toggle should be off by default on a fresh install.

And if an admin enables this toggle, the toggles below it that rely on the lookup server should either stay off by default, or a popup should explicitly ask admins whether or not they want to use the features that rely on the lookup server, explaining that certain parts of their users' profiles will be shared with this server, and how their users can control which parts are shared.

I, at least, was always under the impression that these federation settings would only matter if I explicitly used federation, i.e. if I actively trusted other servers. So even if users had certain things set to federated in their profiles (which, btw, shouldn't be set that way as a default either), it never occurred to me that any data would be sent to a third party server. I even had the federation app disabled on one server and I still saw the requests from <redacted-host> in the Apache log.

So again, please disable all federation features by default, and clearly inform admins when they enable certain federation features that data will be sent to your servers.

And please do not assume that as developers, especially of self-hosted software, you are automatically part of your users' circle of trust and can therefore decide for them what they should consider secure or private. If we didn't want to make those decisions for ourselves, we wouldn't host our own servers.

Thanks! 😊

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
For everyone in general and @reporter in particular as the reporter

# Current state of the investigation and release timeline for server

The Lookup server does not and never did store any data of users unless they had opted-in in their personal settings by setting some (at least one) or all of their data to 'published' and only that data together with the usedID would than be stored.

Due to a logic issue in the February 2025 releases of the Nextcloud server, the server sent unnecessary requests to the Lookup server.

To add a bit more detail: We suspect that this flood of requests was caused by a change that was designed to clean up user data. It would trigger a "data has changed", resulting in the Nextcloud server to contact the Lookup server. It would send a request for all users who had any of their data ever set to 'published'. Moreover, it would also send a `DELETE` request for the data of all users with untouched account details since February 2021.

For each user, the Lookup server then follows up with a `http` request to verify the authenticity of the request. The request leaks the Federated Cloud ID of the user and should use `https` when available. This follow-up is also not needed when users have no data on the Lookup server, and we will change this logic.

At least until these two issues are fixed we will keep the lookup server disabled.

We will also investigate the report that the deletion on the lookup server does not work.

---

Nevertheless to still for the moment ensure no outbound calls to the lookup server happen to store data this logic will generally be deactivated in-code for the upcoming 

* *maintenance release scheduled for 13th March* with
* *release candidates scheduled for 11th March*.

Moin @reporter !

So the short answer is no but this will be implemented before we bring back the lookup solution. 

In a lengthier version: No or rather complicated to do for the admin by unpublishing it for all the fields on published for each user where this is the case with the feature on active via the impersonation app for example (impersonation being something you might not want for other reasons in the same field of security/privacy). There is a however:

* This wouldn't work in the current situation with the feature to be completely deactivated
* We won't bring the feature back in any without the mechanisms you mentioned (as said in the beginning)

---

When bringing it back it will be ensured before re-launching that any scenario that one can think of will be covered, currently we are also in discussions with the data protection consultancy how to handle the case where a server admin just takes down the whole server, i.e. deprovisioning the machine, where we need a mechanism that allows to detect data that should be deleted even though we never received an opt-out. One idea was that lookup-server checking back with the Nextcloud instances but we didn't like that approach but are brainstorming how it can be done the other way around rather a resend of a "keep-alive" for records by the Nextcloud instance to the Lookup server and if that doesn't happen for not yet defined amount of time we proactively delete the data cause the age of a record is no indication, if a server is active for i.e. 10 years and a user has opted-in and never changes it would still be valid. Other thing could be to thinks about i.e. a yearly per-user ping to review the visibility settings and on top hit a "still opted-in button" or always show an opt-out button as a short cut and just ask for a review and if the button isn't hit, there is no delete request.

So there are a lot of ideas already while I still want the devs to focus on fully resolving the current matter at hand and get releases out before working on improving a taken down feature/component/mechanism for an improved revival.

---

- the feature being 'a bit unclearly described' in the knobs to turn it on/off
- The on by default-thing
- The interface does not provide sufficient information to individual instance users regarding data processing when they do opt in
- The feature leads to data sharing (even if intentionally clicked by an operator fully aware of the processing that then takes place) with an (in my opinion) insufficient/absent data processing agreement.

That is, essentially, up to you. There are probably also several other steps you have to undertake internally which might be better tracked elsewhere (like the mandatory reporting to the DPA etc.); And, as with any 'big' ticket, it might always make sense if you split a ticket into the individual actionable components, given that the ticket here is more of an 'ongoing investigation' ticket.

comments.body:
# Closing statement

## In short

* The triggering business-logic error on the Nextcloud server-side has been fixed with the March maintenance releases (29.0.13, 30.0.7, 31.0.1, plus enterprise releases for customer), by blocking the calls to the lookup-server
* The callback issue on the lookup-server has been temporarily resolved by taking down lookup-server, not exposing/accepting data since 4th March
* The federated cloudID falsely kept by the lookup-server after processing a delete request of all user profile data of a user has been deleted from its database along with any backup the only remaining backup is a fresh one created _after_ the deletion (so the remaining records are record where the respective user gave consent to store the profile information/fields)

## Follow-Up

As per comments above there are follow-up issues in terms of internally tracked tasks still to be completed as well as things needed to be implemented before bringing back the public/central lookup-server that leaked the federated CloudID via a callback to the Nextcloud server that originally called the lookup server with i.e. a `DELETE` request or create/update while the formerly mentioned delete-requests and a business-logic error in the maintenance releases of February 2025 triggered this spike in the creation of delete requests which led to spotting this issues.

The follow-up work items will be tracked in dedicated Github issues on the server repository (this one) as well as the lookup-server repository (https://github.com/nextcloud/lookup-server/)
